newsitem.title: UK: Dunblane parents plead with MPs for handgun ban.
newsitem.headline: Dunblane parents plead with MPs for handgun ban.

text.p: Parents of children shot dead in the Dunblane massacre last March pleaded with British members of parliament to opt for a complete ban on handguns in a crucial vote on Monday.

Scotland's top-selling Daily Record newspaper flew a party of Dunblane residents to London to lobby members of parliament to oppose a partial ban proposed by the government of Prime Minister John Major.
The group was headed by Ann Pearston, organiser of the Snowdrop petition for stricter gun laws, which has attracted the signatures of 750,000 Britons.

The government is attempting to push a bill through parliament which would ban all handguns with a calibre higher than .22, but permit individuals to own smaller weapons provided they were kept in secure conditions in gun clubs.

"If the wrong decision is made tonight, what you will get is more deaths and more victims and more people whose lives are ruined -- and I mean ruined," Pearston told a news conference attended by MPs from all the main British political parties.
MPs are expected to vote at or before midnight (2400 GMT) on an amendment put forward by four rebel Conservatives calling for a total ban.

"We have the opportunity in this country to show the rest of the world that in any decent society, there is no place for handguns," Rodney Mayor, whose teacher wife Gwen was killed at Dunblane along with 16 pupils, told the news conference.

Eileen Harrild, another teacher at the Dunblane school where crazed loner Thomas Hamilton struck, told journalists: "These weapons (smaller calibre handguns) are designed to kill, they are lethal and we would like to see them all banned."

Major has ordered Conservative MPs to vote for his government's proposal, which he says will allow target shooting to continue. Ministers expect MPs will narrowly reject a total ban and avoid an embarrassing defeat for Major.

The Conservatives have a majority of just one seat in the 651-member lower House of Commons, but the handful of rebel Conservatives could be matched by a small number of MPs from opposition parties backing a partial ban.
Robert Hughes, one of the four Conservatives backing the amendment, said the government's distinction between lower and higher calibre weapons was illogical since both could kill.
